newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Supervisors set principles for interest management.
newsitem.headline: Supervisors set principles for interest management.

text.p: International banking supervisors on Tuesday released a set of general principles on how banks should manage risks from adverse shifts in interest rates.

The principles, which stress the need for adequate risk management practices, were issued by the Basle Commmittee on Banking Supervision, an authoritative body that groups banking regulators from the Group of 10 (G10) nations and Luxembourg.

Supervisors want banks to apply the principles to every aspect of their business that is sensitive to interest rate changes, whether positions are part of the trading book or whether they are traditional money lending or deposit taking.

"It is essential that banks have a comprehensive risk management process in place that effectively identifies, measures, monitors and controls interest rate exposures, and that is subject to appropriate board and senior management oversight," the Committee's report said.
The consultative proposal by the Basle Committe is being sent to banks and supervisors worldwide, which are asked to return any comments to the Committee by April 15, 1997.

G10 comprises the United States, Japan, Canada, Germany, France, Italy, Britain, Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland. Basle Committee guidelines are not only followed by G10 countries, but in most countries worldwide.
The report builds on an attempt by supervisors in April 1993 to develop a common approach to measure interest rate risks.

But this attempt has now been abandoned in favour of principles that reflect supervisors' current strategy of improving the quality of bank management and risk measurement systems instead of trying to micro-manage banks.

The proposed principles are less strict, but in most aspects similar to the qualitative standards supervisors want banks to apply when they use a model-based approach to calculate capital charges under the Basle Capital Accord.
Interest rate risks, or a bank's exposure to adverse movements in interest rates, are a normal part of banking, but excessive risk can pose a significant threat to bank earnings.
Changes in interest rates not only affect how much banks earn in interest income, a important component in a bank's profits, but also the value of a bank's assets.
"Accordingly, an effective risk management process that maintains interest rate risk within prudent levels is essential for the safety and soundness of banks," the report said.

Sound management of interest rate risks by banks involve four basic elements: Appropriate board and senior management oversight, adequate risk management policies, appropriate risk measurement and monitoring systems and internal controls and independent external audits, the supervisors said.

The Basle Committee said it was not planning to ask banks to set aside capital specifically for interest risks as this is already covered by the amendment to the Capital Accord, which will take effect at the end of 1997.

However, the report noted that individual supervisors may decide to apply capital charges to a banking system, or to individual banks that are more extensively exposed to interest rate risks, or whose management is unsatisfactory.
